analysis.one_liner: Caps the total cost federal rules can impose on businesses and voids rules exceeding the cap.
analysis.headline: Introduced by two Senate Republicans in July 2022, the bill never got a committee vote and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a yearly dollar cap — a "regulatory budget" — on the total cost that federal agencies' rules can impose on businesses, nonprofits, and state and local governments. A new executive-branch Office of Regulatory Analysis would estimate each proposed rule's costs, and no agency could issue a rule that pushes it over its cap; any rule issued in violation would have no force and could be struck down by any party in court. The bill also delays most new rules by at least 75 days, brings agency guidance documents with $25 million or more in costs under the cap, and removes notice-and-comment exemptions for interpretive rules and policy statements.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses, trade associations, and other regulated entities would gain a hard ceiling on new federal regulation. A company facing a costly new safety, environmental, or financial rule could go to court to void it if the agency exceeded its cap, and the new Office could effectively block rules by refusing to certify them. Agencies would have to offset every new rule's costs by deregulating elsewhere, regardless of how much benefit the rule delivered.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a national regulatory budget that sets a maximum on the regulatory costs all executive branch agencies combined — and each agency individually — may impose in a fiscal year.

Bars an agency from issuing any covered rule unless the new Office of Regulatory Analysis determines the rule will not push the agency over its cost cap; a rule issued in violation has no force or effect, and any party may sue to have it declared void.

Prohibits most covered rules from taking effect until at least 75 days after the agency submits the proposal to the Office, except where public health, safety, or national security requires faster action.

Expands the definition of a rule to include agency guidance and directives that cost regulated entities $25 million or more per year, and removes existing notice-and-comment exemptions for interpretive rules and general statements of policy.
Requires an annual Report on National Regulatory Costs, including costs imposed on small businesses, and directs the Office to recommend rules for streamlining or repeal.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal rules would bear the cost. Because the budget counts only costs and never benefits, agencies would have to trade away existing protections — on workplace safety, clean air and water, consumer finance, food safety — to make room for any new one, no matter how valuable. A single presidentially appointed Director would get a 60-day window in which failure to certify a rule kills it, and state and local governments would count as regulated entities whose costs are capped.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, workers, and communities relying on federal rules

drawbacks.text: The cap is defined entirely in terms of costs to regulated entities — direct costs and regulatory costs — with no accounting for the benefits a rule produces, so a rule whose benefits far exceed its costs would still force the agency to strip out an equal amount of protection elsewhere.

It hands a single presidentially appointed Director a mandatory gate over rulemaking: an agency may not promulgate a covered rule unless the Director certifies within 60 days that it fits under the cap, and a rule issued without that certification is void and open to challenge by any party.

Agencies that fail to provide the Office with information face an automatic 0.5 percent sequestration of their appropriations, with waiver authority for historically non-compliant agencies removed — a structural pressure on agencies to satisfy the Office.

Supporters' premise is that regulatory costs are real and often hidden, and that forcing agencies to budget them would prioritize the most valuable rules; an honest supporter would also have to concede that cost estimates are uncertain and that the mechanism binds agencies even when Congress has deliberately authorized a protective rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-facing pieces — an annual report on regulatory costs, published methodologies that outside researchers can replicate, and attention to costs on small businesses — are useful on their own. But the centerpiece is a binding cost cap that counts benefits nowhere, treats cost estimates as fixed facts, and gives one appointee effective veto power over federal rulemaking with a private right of action to void rules. For a country whose federal rules protect workers, consumers, and the environment, the drawbacks outweigh the reporting tools by a wide margin.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, never received any hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the National Regulatory Budget Act of 2022 in the Senate on July 21, 2022, joined by one cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Regulated industries are better off because the bill died: no binding cap on new federal rules was ever created, and agencies retained their existing rulemaking authority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated industries and existing rulemaking authority

sides.party_line_note: Only two Senate Republicans sponsored the bill and no Democrat signed on; it never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals, and other compliance-heavy industries)
industries.note: The bill would give these industries a hard dollar ceiling on the cost of new federal rules, a 75-day delay on most new rules, and a court remedy to void rules issued above the cap. Their gain comes from fewer or weaker public protections, since the cap ignores the benefits rules deliver to consumers, workers, and communities.

The bill counts small businesses among regulated entities whose costs are capped and requires annual reporting of regulatory costs on small businesses, which could ease compliance burdens. But small firms also benefit from federal rules on product safety, credit, and fair dealing that the cap could crowd out.

Agencies would lose control of rulemaking to a new Office of Regulatory Analysis that must certify every covered rule, face a mandatory 75-day delay, and have 0.5 percent of appropriations sequestered for failing to cooperate. Since these agencies carry out the protections the public relies on, hobbling them is a loss for ordinary people.
